6	\label{sec:method}

8	We present OntoCoDec, a framework that compiles IE ontologies into token-level constraints enforced during autoregressive generation.
9	The design is guided by a decidability analysis of IE type constraints.
10	
11	\paragraph{Constraint decidability taxonomy.}
12	\label{sec:decidability}
13	We classify IE type constraints into three levels: (1)~\emph{context-free}: vocabulary membership and JSON structure; (2)~\emph{prefix-decidable with state}: domain/range type validity, determined at each type-bearing position given the decoded relation type and entity registry; (3)~\emph{non-local}: cross-entity type consistency, which depends on the full output.
14	Unlike code generation where types are statically declared, IE constraints fall into level~2: entity types are inferred from text, the registry is built dynamically, and constraint targets depend on the co-occurring relation.
15	OntoCoDec guarantees levels 1--2 (grammar and semantic layers, respectively); level~3 is addressed by beam search or post-hoc resolution (Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).
16	
17	\smallskip
18	\noindent
19	Existing grammar-constrained decoding frameworks (e.g., XGrammar) enforce level~1 constraints---structural validity and vocabulary membership---but IE domain/range rules require cross-position entity-type state that context-free grammars cannot express.
20	We formalize this gap:
21	
22	\smallskip
23	\noindent\textbf{Proposition 1} (Level 2 $\not\subseteq$ Level 1)\textbf{.}
24	\textit{Domain/range type constraints for IE with unbounded entity sets are not context-free.}
25	
26	\smallskip
27	\noindent\textit{Proof sketch.}
28	Consider $\mathcal{E} = \{\tau_A, \tau_B\}$ and a relation $r$ with $\operatorname{dom}(r) = \{\tau_A\}$.
29	An output contains $n$ entities with independently chosen types ($a_i \in \{A, B\}$), followed by a relation referencing head $e_k$ for arbitrary $k \leq n$.
30	Validating the head-type field requires retrieving $\tau_{a_k}$, the type assigned at position $k$ in the entity list.
31	A PDA's LIFO stack cannot retrieve position $k < n$ without destroying entries above it; since both $n$ and $k$ are independently unbounded, no PDA can enforce this constraint for all valid outputs.
32	OntoCoDec's semantic layer addresses this with a runtime entity registry $\mathcal{D}$ (a finite map enabling random-access type lookups), operating as a deterministic stateful transducer over the token stream.\hfill$\square$
33

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion
% Full discussion in Appendix; Mistral boundary condition in app:dual-factor.

OntoCoDec formally compiles IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints via a decidability-guided architecture: LoRA + greedy S1 achieves DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%, CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\%; beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violations on SciERC (1.54$\times$ latency); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% for calibrated models.
$\bar{\kappa}$ characterizes constraint regimes, with entity type confusability as the critical co-factor (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa-case-study}); the decidability taxonomy and $\bar{\kappa}$ diagnostic yield a principled deployment workflow.

\section{Reproducibility Details}
\label{app:reproducibility}

\paragraph{Fine-tuning configuration.}
All four fine-tuned models (Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on SciERC and DocRED) use identical LoRA hyperparameters: rank $r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, dropout $0.05$, no bias, targeting all attention and MLP projection layers (\texttt{q\_proj}, \texttt{k\_proj}, \texttt{v\_proj}, \texttt{o\_proj}, \texttt{gate\_proj}, \texttt{up\_proj}, \texttt{down\_proj}).
Training uses AdamW with learning rate $2{\times}10^{-4}$, cosine schedule, warmup ratio $0.1$, effective batch size $16$, bf16 precision, gradient checkpointing, and completion-only loss for 3 epochs.
SciERC trains on 1,762 examples (260 dev) for 333 steps; DocRED trains on 3,053 examples (998 dev) for 573 steps.
Maximum sequence length is 2,048 (SciERC) and 4,096 (DocRED).
All runs use seed 42.

\paragraph{Hardware and software.}
Training runs on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU (98\,GB VRAM).
SciERC fine-tuning takes approximately 11 minutes per model; DocRED takes approximately 1.5 hours.
Software versions: PyTorch 2.10, Transformers 4.57, PEFT 0.19, TRL 1.1, Accelerate 1.13.

\paragraph{Inference time.}
Inference timing is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:runtime} (NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU, same hardware as training).
Full S1 constrained decoding adds $+$13.1\% wall-clock overhead on SciERC and $+$2.43\% on DocRED (Qwen3-8B, zero-shot greedy); under LoRA fine-tuning, overhead is $+$10.0\% on SciERC.

\paragraph{Greedy decoding determinism.}
\label{app:greedy-determinism}
% exp_id: d067_seed_variance
All main results use greedy decoding (temperature$\,{=}\,$0, argmax token selection).
Argmax is deterministic: the random seed controls \texttt{torch.manual\_seed} for sampling and dropout, neither of which is active during greedy inference.
We verify this with three seeds (42, 123, 456) across two LoRA fine-tuned models on all 551 SciERC documents.
Seeds 123 and 456, evaluated on the same GPU, produce byte-identical outputs for both Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B.
The residual variance in Table~\ref{tab:seed-variance} stems entirely from cross-hardware floating-point divergence: seed 42 was evaluated on a different server with a different CUDA driver version.
Even under this conservative upper bound, $\sigma(\text{E-F1}) \leq 0.16$\,pp, $\sigma(\text{R-F1}) \leq 0.43$\,pp, and $\sigma(\text{DR\%}) \leq 0.08$\,pp.
The constrained decoding DR\% reduction ($-$2.06\,pp for Qwen, $-$1.01\,pp for Llama) exceeds this variance by ${>}12\times$ (signal-to-noise ratio ${>}$\,12), confirming that observed improvements reflect genuine method effects rather than run-to-run noise.
We therefore report single-run results without error bars; bootstrap confidence intervals (10{,}000 iterations) are provided for F1 metrics.

\label{tab:seed-variance}

\midrule

\paragraph{Beam search non-determinism.}
Greedy decoding is deterministic (\S\ref{app:greedy-determinism} above).
Beam search ($k{\geq}2$) introduces non-determinism from GPU floating-point accumulation order; we report single-run results.
Based on the greedy cross-hardware variance ($\sigma < 0.5$\,pp, Table~\ref{tab:seed-variance}), beam search variance is expected to be of similar magnitude.
